ai_summary:
Scotland's electricity network highlights a stark operational divergence between regional clean generation and national balancing requirements. Scottish carbon intensity stands at 0 gCO2/kWh, markedly outperforming the 134 gCO2/kWh recorded GB-wide. This performance is underpinned by strong renewable generation, with estimated Scottish wind output reaching 4.8 GW, representing 47.5% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Across the wider system, total GB wind output stands at 13.1 GW.

However, cross-border transmission limits severely constrain the delivery of this clean electricity to major demand centres. Scottish generation curtailed so far today has reached 28296.3 MWh, imposing a constraint cost of about £691,407 on the system. This curtailment creates adverse environmental impacts downstream, as zero-carbon Scottish electricity must be substituted by fossil generation elsewhere. Specifically, an estimated 5376297.0 m3 of gas was burned elsewhere to replace it, leading to 9903.7 tonnes CO2 being emitted into the atmosphere. These outcomes reinforce the ongoing friction between high Scottish renewable capacity and grid bottlenecks, where curtailing zero-carbon power elevates consumer costs and prompts carbon-intensive balancing across the wider network.
